findings.detail: `PRICE_HEADERS` flattens `'retail price'` and its synonyms (`regular price`, `selling price`, `price`) into one unordered Set, and `findKey` returns the FIRST row key that matches in `Object.keys` order. `resolveSourceKey` in templateMapping.ts deliberately tries the exact header first and only then the synonyms in listed order, precisely so a row carrying both `Price` and `Retail Price` maps the latter — and the module header states the whole point of templateMapping is that the mapper and the exporter 'can never disagree about which extracted column feeds which template column'. A row where the model emits `Price` before `Retail Price` now has the range rule applied to `Price` (which the HEADER_SYNONYMS comment itself notes is usually the purchase cost on an invoice extraction) while `Retail Price` keeps the range text and exports unchanged. Narrow trigger — the OCR prompt asks for `Retail Price` by name — which is why this is low rather than medium; it would rise if invoice extractions routinely returned both columns. The same applies to `DESCRIPTION_HEADERS` at line 42.
findings.summary: findKey uses a flat synonym Set, losing templateMapping's exact-before-synonym precedence

findings.detail: `applyPriceRanges` returns a well-typed `PriceRangeResult` whose `rows` is `Record<string, unknown>[]`, but the new lines re-widen it: `const resultArray: any[] = ranged.rows` (402), `let result: any[] = []` (461), and the two `(r: any) =>` predicates at 400/463. The file is pervasively `any` already, so this is idiomatic here rather than a regression — but it discards type information the PR itself just created, which is the one case the strict-mode handbook asks a reviewer to push back on. None of the four carries an inline justification comment.
findings.summary: New `any` annotations added where the source type is now known

findings.detail: `const key = findKey(rows[idx[0]], PRICE_HEADERS)!` asserts away a `.find()` that can return undefined. It is provably safe — the grouping loop at 179-186 only pushes an index when `findKey` returned a key for that same row — so this is an observation, not a defect. It is called out only because it is exactly the shape the type-safety handbook lists, and the proof lives ten lines away where a future reader will not look.
findings.summary: Non-null assertion on a `.find()` result in the merge loop
